title: The Peace Offering: A Meal Shared with God
summary: Leviticus 3 gives the rules for the peace offering, an animal sacrifice from the herd or the flock that a worshiper brings freely. The steps are the same for cattle, sheep, and goats: the offerer lays a hand on the animal and slaughters it, the priests splash its blood against the altar, and the fat around the entrails, kidneys, and liver is burned as the LORD's portion. The chapter closes with a permanent rule that Israel must never eat fat or blood.
story: Leviticus opens where Exodus ends. The tabernacle has just been set up, the cloud of God's glory has filled it, and Moses cannot go in (Exodus 40:34-35). The question hanging over the whole book is how a holy God can live in the middle of a flawed people without that nearness destroying them. Chapters 1 to 7 begin the answer with a manual of offerings. Chapter 1 described the burnt offering, which went up in smoke almost entirely, and chapter 2 the grain offering. Chapter 3 adds the one sacrifice that ordinary worshipers would actually eat. Later instructions (7:11-36) explain the division: the fat goes to God on the altar, the breast and right thigh go to the priests, and the rest is a feast for the offerer and his household. After this chapter the manual turns to the offerings that deal with sin and guilt (chapters 4 to 6). The order is worth noticing. Leviticus describes the meal of peace with God before it describes the remedy for failure.
historical:
Leviticus presents these instructions as words the LORD spoke to Moses from the Tent of Meeting at Mount Sinai (1:1; 7:38), during the month between the tabernacle's completion (Exodus 40:17) and Israel's departure. Tradition credits the material to Moses; many modern scholars assign it to a priestly school whose work reached its final form centuries later, while others argue that the priestly laws are substantially older than the exile. The book introduction sets out these positions. Whatever the date of the writing, the practice it describes is old. Shared sacrificial meals were common across the ancient Near East, and ritual texts from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast destroyed around 1200 BC, list a sacrifice whose name (shlmm) is a close relative of the Hebrew word for this offering.

Israel's later history shows how the rules of Leviticus 3 were meant to work and how they could be bent. At the sanctuary in Shiloh, Elkanah shared the meat of his sacrifice with his wives and children every year (1 Samuel 1:3-5). In the same years Eli's sons, the priests there, sent a servant to seize meat before the fat had been offered. When a worshiper protested, “The fat must be burned first; then you may take whatever you want,” the servant threatened to take it by force (1 Samuel 2:15-16). The narrator's verdict is that they were treating the LORD's offering with contempt. The order laid down in this chapter, God's portion first, was exactly what they refused.
cultural:
Meat was not everyday food for most people in ancient Israel. Flocks and herds were a family's wealth, kept for milk, wool, and labor, and slaughtering an animal usually meant a festival, a guest, or a celebration. The peace offering turned such a meal into worship. The fat named in verses 3 and 4 is the suet packed around the entrails and kidneys, together with the lobe of the liver. It was considered the richest part of the animal, and Hebrew uses the word for fat to mean the best of anything, as when Pharaoh promises Jacob's family that they will eat “the fat of the land” (Genesis 45:18). Giving it to God meant giving him the best portion, and verse 16 says so plainly: “All the fat is the LORD’s.” The sheep of verse 9 belong to the fat-tailed breeds still raised in the Middle East, whose broad tails store a heavy mass of fat that cooks prize.

Two other details would have caught an ancient reader's attention. The text calls the burned portion food (verses 11 and 16), vocabulary Israel shared with its neighbors, whose temples set out daily meals before the statues of their gods. Israel kept the word but not the belief; in a psalm God says, “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine” (Psalm 50:12). And the lobe of the liver was the organ diviners read. Clay models of sheep livers used for divination have been found in Mesopotamia and at Canaanite sites such as Hazor. Some scholars suggest that burning the lobe on the altar kept it out of such use, though the text itself gives no reason.
literary: The chapter is case law, built on if-clauses, and it sets three nearly identical paragraphs side by side: an animal from the herd (verses 1-5), a lamb from the flock (6-11), and a goat (12-16). Each follows the same steps: present the animal, lay a hand on its head, slaughter it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, let the priests splash the blood on all sides of the altar, remove the fat from the entrails, kidneys, and liver, and burn it. The repetition does real work, since the worshiper with an ox and the worshiper with a goat stand on the same footing. Small differences stand out against that sameness. Unlike the burnt offering, which had to be male (1:3, 10), the peace offering may be male or female, and there is no provision for birds. The sheep paragraph adds the fat tail. Then verse 17 steps back from the altar to every Israelite home, turning a ritual detail into a rule for all generations.

outline.t: A peace offering from the herd
A peace offering from the flock: a lamb
A peace offering of a goat
A permanent rule: no fat and no blood

doctrines.note: The peace offering is a covenant meal. God, priest, and worshiper each receive a share of one animal, a picture of relationship enjoyed rather than a debt paid. When the covenant was sealed at Sinai, young bulls were sacrificed as peace offerings and Israel's leaders ate and drank in God's presence (Exodus 24:5, 11).

God claims the first and best portion, and the claim does not stop at the altar. The ban on eating fat and blood in verse 17 applies wherever Israelites live, so every ordinary meal carried a reminder that life and its best gifts belong to God.

Verse 17 is called a permanent statute. Later passages give its reasons: blood carries the life that belongs to God and is given for atonement on the altar (17:11), and the fat of sacrificial animals is his portion (7:23-25).

words.note: Shelem, peace offering, almost always used in the plural (shelamim). Most scholars connect it with shalom, meaning peace, wholeness, and well-being, though the exact sense is debated. Translations show the options: peace offering (BSB, KJV), fellowship offering (NIV), and sacrifice of well-being (NRSV). Leviticus presents it less as a payment to obtain peace than as a celebration by people already at peace with God.

Chelev, fat, meaning the hard suet around the internal organs rather than the fat marbled through the meat, which Israelites could eat. The same word means the best part of anything, such as the finest wheat or oil. That double sense explains why this fat is God's portion in every sacrifice.

Nichoach, soothing or pleasing, always paired with the word for aroma. The phrase first appears in Genesis 8:21, where the LORD smells Noah's offering after the flood and resolves never again to curse the ground. It describes God's favorable acceptance of a gift, not a hunger being satisfied.

christ: The New Testament does not tie Jesus to the peace offering by name the way it does with the sin offering, so the links here are thematic rather than predictive. Paul says of Christ, “For He Himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and says that God reconciled all things to himself “by making peace through the blood of His cross” (Colossians 1:20). When Paul explains the Lord's Supper, he reaches for Israel's sacrificial meals: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?” (1 Corinthians 10:18). The peace offering is the Old Testament's clearest picture of that communion, a sacrifice that ends in a meal eaten in God's presence. Ephesians 5:2 describes Christ's self-giving as “a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,” language that recalls the pleasing aroma of Leviticus 3. Christians have long seen the Lord's Table as the meal that follows the one sacrifice, eaten by people who have been given peace rather than people trying to earn it.

hard.q: Why the insistence on fat and blood, and does the ban still apply to Christians?
hard.a:
The two parts of verse 17 have different roots. The blood rule is older than Sinai: after the flood God tells Noah, “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4), and Leviticus later explains that life is in the blood and that God has given it for atonement on the altar (17:11). Blood belongs to God because life does. The fat rule marks the best part of the sacrificial animals as God's portion. Jewish practice has kept both, removing blood from meat and cutting away forbidden fat.

Christians have answered the question of their own practice in more than one way. The Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to abstain from blood (Acts 15:20, 29). Many interpreters read that as a request suited to its setting, allowing Jewish and Gentile believers to share a table, and note that Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Some churches and Christian groups have continued to avoid eating blood as a standing command. Behind both readings sits the same conviction the chapter teaches: life is a gift from God and is not ours to treat lightly.

questions: The peace offering was a gift that ended in a feast. How does it change your picture of worship to see it as a meal God shares with his people rather than a tax he collects?
The best part of every animal belonged to God. What would it look like to give God the best of your time, attention, or money rather than what is left over?
Eli's sons turned the offering into a way to feed themselves. Where are religious habits most easily bent toward self-interest, in a church or in a single life?
